chapter_theme: Night ends and the sun rises on the wedding morning, the rites are declared complete, and the royal city and the Vidyadhara guests fill the streets with drums, flags, goods and feasting.

cast.role: the male anril birds that call their mates at night
the maid and the youth, the wedded pair
the sun, who climbs and wishes to see the wedding
the crowds of the royal city at the festival
the Vidyadharas who come down to the festival

1062.reading: In the dark before dawn the male anril birds, swollen with longing, gaze at their mates now and then as if they had seen a dream, then embrace them and call softly.
1062.event: The male anril birds cry softly beside their mates as night ends.

1063.reading: As the night wears on, the winds that stir the water-lily ponds blow, the bride and groom are gone, and the whole world sunk in thick darkness has fallen asleep.
1063.nuance: The couple are named only as கன்னியுங் காளையும், the maid and the youth, and the verse says they are away without saying where.
1063.event: The world sleeps while the wedded pair have withdrawn.

1064.reading: Midnight passes and dawn comes in with birdsong, and the thick darkness thins slowly, like the harm done by the bright moon going.
1064.nuance: The simile makes the fading dark the moon's own fault departing; the sense of தீமை here is not sure.

1065.reading: At dawn the birds sound, the swans, startled by the crocodile-lute, give up their sweet notes, and the eastern horizon over the sea turns pale.
1065.event: Birds and swans wake and the east grows pale.

1066.reading: The sun's rays plant themselves in the sky and the spread light hides itself by the hand, as small chiefs turn back when a king rules by command.
1066.nuance: The simile sets the sun as a king whose command makes petty rivals draw back; it is one of the poet's royal comparisons for nature.
1066.event: The sun rises and the other lights recede.

1067.reading: At daybreak the white conches call, lotuses revel in honey, bees that slept hidden in the flowers hum, and honey-rain falls on the dense grove.
1067.event: The morning wakes the conches, lotuses and bees.

1068.reading: The sun climbs in a crowd of rays, saying that he would see the bride, bright as a lit lamp, circling the fire with her bridegroom.
1068.nuance: The sun is given a wish: to see the fire-circling of the wedding. This ties the sunrise to the wedding that the chapter's name and the next verses lay out.
1068.event: The sun rises to watch the marriage rites.

1069.reading: As the sun drinks the water, snow melts from the rocks, hot rays burn the lilies on the pools and the quarters grow wide, as if the face of the world turned.
1069.event: Day grows hot and the pools wither.

1070.reading: The poet says that the rites of the wedding were completed by good law, and leaves the account of what happened to the groom and bride to those who can tell it.
1070.nuance: The verse is a narrator's turn: the marriage is done and he declines to describe its detail. The word division is damaged.
1070.event: The wedding rites are completed, and the poet leaves the telling of them.

1071.reading: On the day of worship of the feet of the lord who has three umbrellas, drums were beaten on dark elephants carrying heavy gold.
1071.nuance: Whom the 'lord of three umbrellas' (the Arhat) is, is taken from the epic's setting; the verse gives only the title and the drums.
1071.event: Drums are beaten on elephants to announce the worship day.

1072.reading: The streets of the royal city fill with drums, crowds of drummers, incense, smoke, flowers and the food of the offering.
1072.event: The city's streets fill with festival sounds and offerings.

1073.reading: Mares, elephants and others crush together, flags, parasols, whisks and crown-light cover the sky, and there is no room even to tread.
1073.event: Crowds, animals and standards fill the streets.

1074.reading: The people of the city, kept in the road without fault, adorn it for the festival, and drums rise at once for the wedding day.
1074.event: The city is adorned for the wedding day.

1075.reading: The procession lines move by stages, from the Nandi face to the holy water, the afternoon, the chants and the guard's duty.
1075.nuance: The verse works as a list of the day's stages named by the word மாலை; the exact sense of each stage is held loosely.
1075.event: The wedding ceremony proceeds in set stages through the day.

1076.reading: Sounds of the sea, of drums and of the court rise together in so great a din that none can tell the one from the other.
1076.nuance: The verse has only three lines in the printed text, so a line may be lost; the sense is held loosely.
1076.event: Sea, drums and court rise in one noise.

1077.reading: Young women with pearl-white laughter and red lips shed pearls from their eyes, which mix with the sand and fill the streets.
1077.event: Young women's pearls fill the sand of the street.

1078.reading: Banners rise, incense smoke fills the air, and night joins day so that night and day agree in the city.
1078.event: Incense and flags turn night to day.

1079.reading: Songs and dances stood together, and kings of the earth and kings of ancient clans slept in the cool on the great mountain.
1079.event: Kings sleep on the mountain after the songs and dances.

1080.reading: Sky-dwellers and Vidyadharas descend in crowds from the heavens, and the golden city shines like stars scattered with the sun.
1080.event: Sky-dwellers and Vidyadharas come down to the golden city.

1081.reading: The Vidyadharas look with joy at the golden lotuses opening on the northern peak and in the pond.
1081.event: The Vidyadharas look at golden lotuses.

1082.reading: The streets spread with goods for the festival: jewels laid out for those who wish them, gems cut for those who wish them, and gifts of cloth.
1082.event: Goods are laid out in the streets for the festival.

1083.reading: Some drink toddy and laugh, others take in the food of the gods, others dwell with kin; so the streets filled with such groups.
1083.event: Different crowds feast and gather in the streets.

1084.reading: Vidyadharas pour down from every quarter, a rain of gold falls, and in the rain a whirl of ancient crowds rises, which is not told here.
1084.nuance: The last line says the speaker does not tell more; it ends the chapter on a promise that the full account is omitted.
1084.event: Vidyadharas come down and a rain of gold falls on the festival.

links.note: 1068 sends the sun up to see the fire-circling; 1070 reports the rites complete.
links.teaches: The poet makes the sun a witness, so the unseen wedding is told through daybreak and not in itself.

links.note: 1071 beats the drums for the worship day; 1075 lays out the stages of the day's procession.
links.teaches: The festival's religious worship and its marriage procession share one day and one set of stages.

links.note: Both lay out the city streets full of offering and goods.
links.teaches: The streets are filled first with sound and incense, then with goods, building one festival picture.

source_issues: Verse 1076 has three lines instead of four.
Verses 1062 and 1080 had a line repaired for a stray pulli.
Verses 1070 to 1084 have broken word division in places and several readings are held loosely.
